title: An Execution‑Oriented Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Simulate→Rollback Pipelines for LLM‑Assisted NetOps: a Confirmatory Study with gpt‑5‑mini
abstract: We preregistered (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to test whether a guarded generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline (C) reduces actionable misconfigurations relative to a generation‑only baseline (A) on vendor‑neutral NetOps tasks. Design: N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks (routing/ACL/NAT), model=gpt‑5‑mini, paired shared_initial_generation (one generated candidate per task reused across conditions), deterministic simulator adjudicator, primary estimand = paired difference in actionable misconfiguration proportion, analysis = paired bootstrap (10,000, seed=1729) and McNemar exact. Result: baseline actionable = 0/160; guarded actionable = 0/160; paired difference = 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00]); McNemar p = 1.00. The preregistered target (≥30% relative reduction) is unevaluable here because the shared_initial_generation pairing created a ceiling effect: the single shared candidate per task was non‑actionable for all tasks, leaving no headroom for the guarded pipeline to demonstrate benefit. We release SHA‑256‑verified artifacts (representative hashes below) so results and scoring can be deterministically reproduced, and we discuss concrete design prescriptions (task calibration, independent per‑condition generation, lightweight human adjudication) for informative follow‑ups.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs promise to accelerate NetOps workflows (intent→configuration, change planning, repair), but fluent generations can be operationally unsafe unless surrounded by verification, sandbox enactment, and rollback. Prior work shows verifier and simulator layers can materially reduce unsafe enactments. We asked the preregistered confirmatory research question (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1): does a guarded generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline (C) reduce actionable misconfigurations by ≥30% relative to generation‑only (A) on a representative NetOps confirmatory task set? Our contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, fully artifacted paired confirmatory execution using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic simulator adjudicator; (2) release of SHA‑256‑verified artifacts permitting deterministic reproduction of scoring and statistical inference; (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the preregistered contrast became unevaluable in this run and concrete prescriptions to obtain informative confirmatory evidence.
sections.related_work: Network verification and runtime checking (VeriFlow and successors) pioneered low‑latency invariant checks on forwarding state [https://doi.org/10.1145/2342441.2342452]. Recent LLM→NetOps literature proposes constrained and generate→validate→repair pipelines (MeshAgent, GraphSynth, MNC, Flow‑of‑Action) and new benchmarks (OpsEval, LogEval). Unlike purely capability benchmarks, our experiment ties LLM generation to deterministic simulator enactment and a preregistered paired inferential design, emphasizing an execution‑oriented operational outcome (actionable vs non‑actionable) rather than only language‑level correctness.
sections.methodology: Preregistration: study id c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1 froze task selection (N=160; routing≈64, ACL≈64, NAT/other≈32) drawn from public vendor‑neutral corpora (see cited records), augmentation seeds [42,123,999], model=gpt‑5‑mini, adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1, and the shared_initial_generation policy (one generated candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded). Primary estimand: paired difference in actionable misconfiguration proportion (A − C). Analysis plan: paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) to estimate 95% CI and exact McNemar two‑sided test for paired binary outcomes. Adjudication: a deterministic simulator applied canonicalized configurations and returned an actionable boolean; per‑task scoring JSONs record simulator diagnostics. Retry and stopping rules: up to two transient retries per provider error; planned episodes = 320 (160 paired tasks). All raw outputs, provider call logs, per‑task scoring JSONs, canonicalized configs, and analysis scripts were archived and SHA‑256 hashed; representative hashes (execution manifest) include: execution/raw_results.jsonl = 2445d0f8e9be9cfa34ede1bbe80b82d6f05b51bcafc7c1688d0ed8e1c73d8044; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv = fba3b0ca21c7c7c380ed1134b4fce48b0870bf72a7be0fd8610bf7e6b63a970b. The shared_initial_generation policy was preregistered to reduce generator variance when isolating validator/simulator effects; its operational consequence is central to the observed outcome.

sections.discussion: Why the preregistered hypothesis is unevaluable here. The preregistered shared_initial_generation policy reused a single generated candidate per task across both conditions. When that shared candidate is already non‑actionable according to the deterministic simulator, the guarded pipeline has no opportunity to (a) block, (b) propose repairs, or (c) demonstrate a reduction in actionable outcomes — producing a ceiling effect (n_11=160). This outcome is informative for benchmark design: (1) pairing that suppresses generator variance can remove detectability of downstream pipeline benefits if generator outputs are too good (or the simulator predicate too permissive); (2) confirmatory evaluation must include a task‑calibration step to ensure nonzero baseline actionable rate or use independent per‑condition generation to allow the safety machinery to act. Practical prescriptions for informative follow‑ups: run a small calibration sample to confirm baseline headroom; adopt independent per‑condition generation (separate generation calls per condition) when the scientific question concerns pipeline interventions; include a tiny human adjudication sample to validate simulator actionable semantics. Operational implications: this run does not show guarded pipelines are ineffective; it shows that a particular paired experimental design plus a high generator quality (for the chosen tasks/prompts) produced a degenerate distribution that prevents inference. The archived artifacts permit deterministic re‑scoring and reanalysis under alternative pairing or scoring choices.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered and fully artifacted paired confirmatory experiment comparing generation‑only and guarded generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipelines using gpt‑5‑mini on N=160 vendor‑neutral NetOps tasks. Observed baseline actionable = 0/160 and guarded actionable = 0/160; paired difference = 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.00). The preregistered target (≥30% relative reduction) is unevaluable here because the shared_initial_generation design produced a ceiling effect. The scientific value of the run is the artifact‑grounded diagnosis: confirmatory designs that reuse a single generated candidate per task can suppress the ability to detect downstream pipeline benefits when generators already produce non‑actionable candidates. We publish SHA‑256‑verified artifacts and recommend calibrated, independent‑generation confirmatory designs for future informative evaluations. All principal numbers and scoring JSONs cited above are traceable to the archived files and hashes recorded in the execution manifest and analysis artifacts cited in this manuscript.

disclosure_statement:
Mandatory Disclosure Statement (CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track).

Models and orchestration: primary model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API). Orchestration/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The Master Prompt bundle guiding the autonomous run is the Master Prompt v1 — Autonomous CNSM 2026 Research Run; the Research Director selected the topic family and initial constraints prior to the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: collaborative pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred and were explicitly excluded from final empirical evidence. Autonomy claim: after the autonomy lock, literature review, research‑gap selection, preregistration, prompt generation, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, manuscript drafting, and revision were performed autonomously. No human manually edited the technical manuscript content, numerical results, figures, captions, references, or this Disclosure Statement after the autonomy lock.

Preregistration and frozen design: the run followed preregistration id c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1 which froze the confirmatory paired design, task selection (N=160; augmentation seeds [42,123,999]), shared_initial_generation policy (one candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded), model (gpt‑5‑mini), maximum model calls (320), primary estimand, analysis plan (paired bootstrap 10,000, seed=1729 and McNemar exact), retry policy, and stopping rules. No post‑hoc changes affecting confirmatory inference were made.

Artifact integrity and reproducibility: all raw model outputs, provider call logs, canonicalized configurations, per‑task scoring JSONs, deterministic simulator scoring schema, analysis scripts, and the execution manifest are archived and SHA‑256 hashed. Representative authoritative files and their SHA‑256 values (as recorded in the execution manifest) include: execution/raw_results.jsonl = 2445d0f8e9be9cfa34ede1bbe80b82d6f05b51bcafc7c1688d0ed8e1c73d8044; execution/result_schema.json = 63199db3f7219b969acc5497fae613c8d5df16e081768969f67b7b3024844465; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv = fba3b0ca21c7c7c380ed1134b4fce48b0870bf72a7be0fd8610bf7e6b63a970b. Per‑task scoring JSONs are under execution/scoring/ and are enumerated with SHA‑256 hashes in the execution manifest; those scoring files contain the actionable flag used for primary inference. Example scoring JSON hashes (artifacts used in manuscript text): execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json = e321b84c41233594d2bebc0d01722cade9ab148516fcf13fd9788c94fb638e59; execution/scoring/task-000050-baseline.json = e4fa1208479e3d51adbdb7147ea951766fda52baefee705d2320da8870395d90; execution/scoring/task-000160-baseline.json = 6310438573e09696982a7edd299d12731966266bd66fb1470123f0b1549ba8ef.

Provider calls and retries: planned maximum model calls = 320; actual provider model calls used = 160 because the preregistered shared_initial_generation design used one generation per task. The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two transient retries for provider errors; none materially affected confirmatory outcomes. Provider call audit and call cache entries are recorded in the execution manifest.

Human role limitations: the Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock development. After the autonomy lock, no human performed manual edits to technical content or numeric results. The artifacts and hashes above permit deterministic verification of the run without additional manual manuscript edits.
limitations: Ceiling effect: baseline generation produced zero actionable misconfigurations under the chosen deterministic simulator (baseline = 0/160), making the preregistered ≥30% relative‑reduction target unevaluable.

Shared‑candidate policy: the preregistered shared_initial_generation (one candidate per task used for both baseline and guarded) prevents the guarded pipeline from demonstrating benefit on tasks where the shared candidate is already non‑actionable.
Single‑model scope: conclusions apply to gpt‑5‑mini and the exact prompts/call budget used; multi‑model generality is unresolved.
Construct abstraction: the deterministic simulator predicate is an abstraction and may not capture all production failure modes; a small human adjudication check is recommended for production claims.
No live device enactment: evaluation used a deterministic simulator rather than live production enactment, limiting external validity to production rollouts.
